stemBlocks.value: Three supermarkets sell the same 1.5 L bottle of cooking oil: Super Mart $780 per bottle, Family Foods 3 bottles for $2 250, Budget Store 10% discount on $820. Reduce each offer to a price per bottle and decide which store gives the best buy. (The workbook prints the stem and table only; the lettered parts are not in this extract.)
Think first: Every offer is for the same 1.5 L bottle, so you only need the price of a single bottle in each case.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p022-q26 from workbook page 22.

solutionSteps.instruction: Write down Super Mart's price per bottle.
Divide Family Foods' offer by the number of bottles.
Apply the discount to Budget Store's price.

strategyBlocks.value: Read Super Mart directly, divide Family Foods by 3, apply the 10% discount to Budget Store, then compare the three unit prices.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: Price per bottle: Super Mart $780, Family Foods $750, Budget Store $738. Budget Store offers the best buy.

whyThisWorks.value: Offers can only be compared once they are expressed in the same units, here dollars per bottle. A multi-buy deal and a percentage discount look very different on the shelf, but reducing both to a unit price puts them on one scale. Since all three bottles are the same 1.5 L size, price per bottle ranks the stores exactly as price per litre would.

commonErrors.misconception: Comparing $2 250 with $780 and $820 without dividing by 3.

commonErrors.misconception: Taking 10% of $820 as the price rather than as the discount.

examTip.value: Reduce every offer to the cost of one before comparing anything. It turns a confusing table into three numbers you can simply rank.
